topic: Sound for Picture — Post Workflow & Deliverables

fields.definition: A Foley 'moves' cue that recreates the cloth sounds of a jacket as a character moves, dresses, or gestures, performed in sync to picture and recorded to replace or reinforce the garment's rustle.
fields.plain_english: It is the sound of a jacket rustling as someone moves. A Foley artist makes this sound by hand in a studio while watching the film. It fills in noise the camera mic missed.
fields.purpose_function: It restores the natural clothing sounds a scene needs for realism, which are often thin or missing on the production dialogue tracks, and gives the mix a clean, controllable cloth element.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist wears or handles a jacket and performs its movements in sync with the picture while the Foley mixer records the passes onto dedicated cloth tracks.
common_mistakes: Assuming clothing sounds are captured well enough on the boom and do not need Foley.
Performing moves out of sync so the cloth rustle drifts from the picture.
Recording the jacket too loudly so it distracts from dialogue in the final mix.
scenario_contexts: Replacing missing clothing rustle in a scene shot with a distant boom.
Adding cloth movement for an international M&E version where original incidental sounds are removed.
Reinforcing a character standing up and putting on a jacket before leaving a room.

sources: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A Foley moves/specifics cue that recreates the small metallic sounds of jewelry — such as bracelets, necklaces, rings, or earrings — jingling or clinking as a character moves, recorded in sync to picture.
fields.plain_english: It is the tiny clink and jingle of jewelry as a person moves. A Foley artist makes these sounds by handling real jewelry in time with the film. This adds detail the set microphone may not have caught.
fields.purpose_function: It adds fine, believable detail to a character's movement and wardrobe, and supplies those sounds as clean, separate elements the mixer can place and balance.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist handles bracelets, chains, and similar jewelry props and performs the jingles in sync while the Foley mixer records them to dedicated tracks.
common_mistakes: Overplaying the jingle so it pulls focus from dialogue.
Using jewelry that sounds nothing like what is seen on screen.
Letting the sound drift out of sync with the actor's motion.
scenario_contexts: A close-up of a character adjusting a bracelet or necklace.
Rebuilding jewelry sounds for an M&E track used in dubbing.
Adding jingle to a character wearing many bangles that were silent on the production track.

sources: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A Foley specifics cue that reproduces the metallic jingling and clinking of a set of keys as a character carries, handles, or drops them, performed and recorded in sync to picture.
fields.plain_english: It is the jingle of a bunch of keys, made by hand for a film. A Foley artist shakes or handles real keys in time with the picture. It gives the scene a sharp, clear sound the camera mic often misses.
fields.purpose_function: It provides a crisp, recognizable prop sound that supports action and character, delivered as a separate clean element the re-recording mixer can control.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist jingles a suitable key set in sync with the actor's hand while the Foley mixer records takes onto a specifics track.
common_mistakes: Recording the keys much louder than they would sound in the real space.
Choosing keys whose pitch or number does not match what is on screen.
Missing the exact frame where the keys are picked up or set down.
scenario_contexts: A character unlocking a door as the keys jingle in hand.
Rebuilding the key sound for an international M&E deliverable.
A tense scene where dropped keys need a clear, well-timed jingle.

sources: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: The oversight of a localized (dubbed or voiced) version to ensure the target-language dialogue is accurate in translation, correctly pronounced, and well matched to lip-sync and performance, carried out by a language or dubbing supervisor.
fields.plain_english: It is checking that a film's new-language voices are correct and natural. A supervisor makes sure the translation is right and the words match the actors' lips. This keeps the dubbed version true to the original.
fields.purpose_function: It protects the meaning, tone, and technical fit of a foreign-language version so the localized release feels true to the original for its new audience.
fields.practical_application: During or after dubbing sessions, the language supervisor reviews takes for translation accuracy, pronunciation, and sync, and flags lines that must be re-recorded.
common_mistakes: Assuming a good translation on paper will automatically fit the actor's lip movements.
Skipping pronunciation checks for names and technical words.
Confusing language supervision with simple subtitle proofreading.
scenario_contexts: Overseeing a Spanish dub of a series for accuracy and sync.
Approving pronunciation of character names across all language versions.
Sending flagged lines back for re-recording during a dubbing session.

sources: Purcell, Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: Automated Dialogue Replacement performed for one specific language version of a production, where voice actors re-record dialogue in that language in sync to picture, producing clean, matched lines for that localized release.
fields.plain_english: It is re-recording a film's dialogue in one chosen language. Voice actors watch the picture and speak their lines in sync in a studio. This gives that language its own clean, matched dialogue.
fields.purpose_function: It supplies each target market with sync dialogue in its own language, kept separate from other versions so each can be mixed and delivered on its own.
fields.practical_application: A dubbing studio cues the picture, and voice actors perform lines in the target language to sync while the ADR mixer records them for that version's mix.
common_mistakes: Reusing one language's ADR timing for another without re-checking sync.
Forgetting that each language version needs its own clean recording, not the original mix.
Ignoring differences in line length between languages that break lip-sync.
scenario_contexts: Recording French lines to picture for a French release.
Replacing an on-set foreign line with studio ADR for one market.
Building sync dialogue for a dub that will be mixed over the M&E.

sources: Purcell, Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: The quality-control review of a completed localized (dubbed or subtitled) version to confirm it meets translation, sync, performance, and technical delivery standards before the version is released.
fields.plain_english: It is the final check of a film made for a new language. Reviewers make sure the voices sync, the translation is right, and the file meets the required specs. Only then is that version approved.
fields.purpose_function: It catches sync, translation, and technical faults in a language version before delivery, protecting quality and preventing costly rejects from the distributor.
fields.practical_application: A QC operator watches the localized version against a checklist, logging any sync slips, wrong lines, level problems, or spec errors for fixing.
common_mistakes: Checking only the audio and missing subtitle or spec errors.
Passing a version without comparing sync against the original picture.
Assuming the source master's QC covers the localized version too.
scenario_contexts: Reviewing a German dub before it ships to a broadcaster.
Logging a lip-sync drift found in one reel of a language version.
Confirming loudness and file specs on a localized deliverable.

sources: Purcell, Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures

fields.definition: The recording session in which dialogue for a specific target-language version is captured to picture, producing the localized voice tracks that are later edited and mixed over the program's M&E.
fields.plain_english: It is the studio session where a film's dialogue is recorded in a new language. Voice actors speak their lines in sync with the picture. These new voices later replace the original ones in that version.
fields.purpose_function: It creates the target-language dialogue needed to build a dubbed version, keeping those voices as a clean, separate element for editing and mixing.
fields.practical_application: In a dubbing studio, actors watch the picture and perform lines in the target language while the mixer records takes for later editing over the M&E.
common_mistakes: Recording without a clean M&E to mix the new voices over.
Letting take levels or mic setup drift between actors in a session.
Not matching recorded line length to the on-screen mouth movements.
scenario_contexts: Recording an Italian dub of a feature over several days.
Capturing target-language voices to sync for a streaming release.
Re-recording a few lines a supervisor flagged as off-sync.

sources: Purcell, Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A dialogue-editing or mixing choice to use the lavalier (body-worn) microphone track as the primary source for a line rather than the boom, usually because the lav gives cleaner, closer, or more usable dialogue in that moment.
fields.plain_english: It means picking the tiny clip-on mic as the main sound for a line, not the boom. Editors do this when the clip-on mic sounds cleaner or clearer. It helps get the best, most usable voice for each moment.
fields.purpose_function: It lets the editor choose the best-sounding microphone per line so the finished dialogue is clear and consistent, especially when the boom is blocked, distant, or noisy.
fields.practical_application: While cutting dialogue, the editor auditions the boom and lav for each line and cuts to the lav when it is cleaner, matching level and tone across the switch.
common_mistakes: Switching to the lav without matching its tone to the boom, so the sound jumps.
Forgetting that lavs pick up clothing rustle and mic bumps.
Always favoring one mic instead of choosing per line for the best result.
scenario_contexts: A wide shot where the boom is too far but the lav is close and clean.
A noisy exterior where the lav rejects background better than the boom.
Cutting between boom and lav within a scene to keep dialogue clear.

sources: Purcell, Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures
